nameStory: Hairy nightshade gets its common name from the fine, soft hairs that cover its stems and leaves, giving the plant a slightly fuzzy texture when you touch it. The 'nightshade' part comes from its membership in a plant family that includes many species associated with darkness and mystery, though this particular species is relatively mild-mannered compared to some of its more notorious relatives.
description: Hairy nightshade is a small annual herb that typically grows 1-2 feet tall with branching stems covered in soft hairs. This South American native has small white flowers and produces tiny berries that change from green to yellowish or orange when ripe. It's an introduced species that occasionally pops up in disturbed areas, though it's quite rare in New England with only a handful of documented sightings.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to egg-shaped leaves with wavy or slightly toothed edges, covered in soft hairs that make them feel velvety to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white star-shaped flowers with five pointed petals and bright yellow centers, clustered in small groups along the stems

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Tiny round berries about the size of a pea, starting green and ripening to yellowish or pale orange, often enclosed in papery husks

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing annual with multiple branching stems that spread outward, rarely exceeding 2 feet in height

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Stems covered in fine, soft hairs that give them a distinctly fuzzy texture when rubbed between your fingers

habitat: Look for hairy nightshade in disturbed soils like roadsides, vacant lots, gardens, and agricultural areas. It prefers sunny locations with well-drained soil and often appears as a weedy species in cultivated ground or areas with recent soil disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil warms up, with young plants developing their characteristic hairy leaves.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs in mid to late summer, with the small white star-shaped flowers most abundant during hot weather. Fruits begin developing as flowers fade.
seasonality.fall: Berries ripen to their yellowish-orange color in early fall before the first frost kills the annual plant.
seasonality.winter: Dead plant material may persist but offers no reliable identification features since this is an annual species.

funFact: Despite being in the same plant family as deadly nightshade, hairy nightshade is actually closely related to familiar foods like tomatoes and potatoes - you can see the family resemblance in those distinctive star-shaped flowers with bright yellow centers!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other small nightshades, especially eastern black nightshade, but the soft, velvety hairs covering the stems and leaves of hairy nightshade are distinctive. Memory trick: if it feels fuzzy, it's the hairy one!
contextualKnowledge: The scientific name of this species has a confusing history - it was long misapplied to a different plant entirely, leading to decades of botanical mix-ups. What we now know as true hairy nightshade was sometimes considered just a variety of another species until botanists sorted out the naming confusion.
compareHints: Hairy nightshade differs from eastern black nightshade by its distinctly hairy stems and leaves (black nightshade is mostly smooth). Unlike bittersweet nightshade, it's a low annual herb rather than a climbing vine, and its berries are yellowish rather than bright red. The soft, fuzzy texture is really the key distinguishing feature among New England's nightshades.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other nightshades in New England, bittersweet nightshade is the only one that grows as a climbing vine with purple flowers.
Among New England's nightshades, Carolina horsenettle is the only one covered in sharp prickles, making it instantly recognizable.
Unlike bittersweet nightshade which has purple flowers and grows as a climbing vine, eastern black nightshade has white flowers and grows as a low bushy annual.
Among its nightshade relatives in New England, tomato is easily distinguished by its large, edible red fruit and cultivation in gardens.
Among New England nightshades, buffalo-bur is unmistakable due to its extreme spininess - no other Solanum species is nearly as heavily armed with spines.
Black nightshade differs from its cousin bittersweet nightshade by being much smaller and having white flowers instead of purple ones with swept-back petals.
Unlike its nightshade relatives, potato has compound leaves rather than simple ones, and produces edible underground tubers.

Green nightshade stands apart from its New England nightshade relatives primarily by its persistently green, glossy berries - eastern black nightshade and black nightshade both produce dark purple-black berries when ripe, while bittersweet nightshade produces bright red berries.
Unlike its wild nightshade relatives that grow as weeds in New England, cultivated eggplant is much larger in all aspects - bigger leaves, bigger flowers, and dramatically bigger fruits.

Garden huckleberry differs from other nightshades in New England by its drooping clusters of dark berries and relatively benign nature – unlike bittersweet nightshade with its bright red berries, or the more weedy black nightshade species.
Unlike other nightshades in New England, red buffalo-bur is the most heavily armed with prickles covering every surface.
